The custom-hooks `fix` command runs without patterns, defaulting to `src/**/*.ts`. This is intentional for the vet gate.

Running the full 280-second vet on every agent completion—including pure Q&A—is accidental waste. Marked FIX.

The success path still buffers all stdout and stderr into memory before discarding them. This is unnecessary bloat. Marked FIX.

The success path must still pipe stdout and stderr because the exit code is required. Aborting early once the exit code is known would avoid buffering all output, but undrained streams may block. The exact FIX is still being weighed.

A capped incremental read—keeping only the last 12k characters while draining—would fix memory bloat on both success and failure paths. Re-running failed steps on non-zero exit was rejected as too complex. The remaining open question is whether to ignore stdout and stderr entirely on the success path, since the exit code cannot be predicted beforehand.

The best fix is a ring-buffered stream drain capped at MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS. This avoids storing the full output while still draining pipes on the success path.

On the success path, reading the full test:coverage output is wasted CPU and memory. Ignoring stdout and stderr by default would make the fast path instant. If the process fails, it can be re-run with capture enabled. This doubles the failure cost but keeps the success path lean.

Re-running failed steps on non-zero exit was rejected because it would double the vet cost on the rare failure path.

The ring-buffered stream drain remains the best fix.

`proc.kill()` is safe to call without awaiting `proc.exited`; the promise should resolve normally, and stdout errors are acceptable.

The hook validates the repository state at execution time, so any user file modifications between agent stop and vet are intentional rather than a race condition.

The full-source `fix` pattern in custom-hooks is overly broad but serves as an intentional quality gate, so the vet-stop cost is SKIP. ## Efficiency review

### `.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts`

- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:47-67`** — **FIX** — `runVet()` always buffers full stdout/stderr via `Response(...).text()` before any truncation. On success (lines 86–88) that output is discarded. `bun vet` can emit large build + coverage logs → unbounded memory and drain work on every stop, even when exit code is 0.
- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:47-53`** — **SKIP** — Full `bun vet` on every `status === "completed"` stop is intentional quality gate (build → typecheck → lint/format → custom-hooks fix → test:coverage). Matches zero-tolerance policy; not accidental waste.
- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:79-82`** — **SKIP** — Early return on `aborted`/`error` avoids vet on non-success stops. Good.
- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:58-62`** — **SKIP** — `Promise.all([stdout, stderr, proc.exited])` already concurrent; no missed parallelism inside the hook.
- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:14,54-56`** — **SKIP** — `VET_TIMEOUT_MS` (280s) vs `hooks.json` timeout (300s) leaves ~20s for sleep/teardown; sane margin.
- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:54-56`** — **FIX (minor)** — `proc.kill()` on timeout with no `SIGKILL` fallback or child-tree handling; hung/grandchild processes can burn hook budget until 300s.
- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:10,69-82`** — **FIX (minor)** — `loop_count` is typed but never read. Cursor enforces `loop_limit: 5` externally, so this isn’t extra loops; hook could still skip vet at limit to save one ~280s run on the final attempt.
- **`.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts:69-82`** — **FIX** — No change/no-code guard. Vet runs on every completed turn (Q&A, docs-only, beads-only) → accidental waste vs intentional gate when no TS sources changed.
